r: The applied work is physical: identifying safe brewery equipment operation, selecting and installing pumps, boilers, chillers and vessels, performing basic troubleshooting and mechanical service, and ultimately brewing on a pilot system. These map to O*NET activities like Repairing and Maintaining Mechanical Equipment and Controlling Machines and Processes, the manual, on-site categories that task-exposure research consistently classifies as low-exposure and that observed-usage data shows barely represented in current AI use. A model can suggest a troubleshooting checklist or size a heat exchanger, but it cannot turn a wrench, diagnose a leaking gasket by feel, or safely bring a hot-side system online. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire hands-on mechanical and process competence on real brewery equipment is unaffected; embodiment does the protective work here, not any licensure mandate.

By 2031, diagnostic software and sensor-driven predictive maintenance will be more capable and may inform how a brewer schedules service or specifies equipment, augmenting the planning layer of this course. But the graded competence, physically operating, servicing, and troubleshooting brewhouse machinery and executing a pilot brew, remains embodied and safety-critical, exactly the work the jagged-frontier evidence warns against trusting to an ungrounded system where a confident wrong call on a pressurized vessel carries real consequences. Diffusion of capable maintenance automation into small craft breweries is slow and uneven. There is no licensure or accreditation lock doing the work; the constraint is that the task itself is manual. The instrumental case is essentially intact at five years, with the honest caveat that more of the design-and-selection analysis may migrate to AI tools.

A decade out, robotics and instrumented brewhouses will absorb more routine monitoring and some maintenance in larger, capital-rich production settings, and AI equipment-selection tools will be strong. Even so, the specific competence Brewery Mechanics builds, a student personally acquiring the physical skill to install, service, and troubleshoot brewing equipment and to run a pilot system, is not a task AI performs on the learner's behalf, and embodiment keeps direct substitution low through 2036 in the central case. The plausible ten-year shift is in how much design calculation and diagnostics are AI-assisted, not in whether hands-on mechanical competence is still needed; craft-scale breweries in particular retain manual, human-serviced equipment. The rating holds Low, with wide uncertainty applying to the automation of large-plant maintenance rather than to this course's embodied training.
BREW 2350.d: In this course, students identify the fundamental aspects of safe operation of a brewery. Activities include the basic principles for design and operation of equipment. Students perform basic troubleshooting and services to equipment. A cumulative course project results in student identification and selection of equipment and process of a brewery by type and style. At course completion, students implement their brewery design by brewing their beer on a pilot brewing system.

r: The course splits between exposed knowledge work and embodied practice. Students investigate malting, fermentation and aging as they relate to historical and modern beer styles, apply pairing principles, and, critically, practice the sensory taste experience to map how flavor relates to style and service. The analytical strand (Getting Information, Analyzing Data or Information, comparing historical styles to the U.S. craft industry) resembles appreciation-course content that task-exposure research places among the more exposed writing-and-explanation activities. But the perceptual tasting competence is in-person and real-time, an embodied evaluation AI does not perform for the learner. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact: a model can summarize beer history or draft pairing notes, yet the course's cultivated palate and stylistic judgment are not delegable, and the sensory component dampens exposure. Rating Low.

By 2031, language models will fluently generate style descriptions, brewing-history synthesis, and pairing guidance, eroding the rationale for producing that written knowledge oneself. The instrumental case shifts toward the student's own sensory literacy and toward critically evaluating AI-generated style claims. The dampening embodiment of tasting keeps the course from tracking fully with exposed writing tasks, but the substantial informational core rises with capability, moving the rating to Medium. There is no licensure lock; the course is a prerequisite substrate for downstream sensory and service courses, which caps erosion only modestly. The honest hedge: how much of knowing beer styles collapses into an instantly queryable reference versus remaining a cultivated human competence is genuinely uncertain, but the analytical half is clearly more automatable by five years.

A decade out, AI will be an authoritative explainer of beer styles, history, and pairing, and the information-delivery rationale for that half of the course is substantially eroded in the central case. What resists is the perceptual, embodied tasting competence, discriminating and mapping flavor to style in real time, which the model does not supply to the learner. With no institutional lock and only modest foundational scaffolding, the rating holds Medium rather than falling to Low: the knowledge strand is highly automatable while the sensory strand is not, and the two are roughly balanced in the description. The wide-uncertainty caveat concerns how such courses are taught when style knowledge is a free lookup, not whether the trained palate remains a genuinely human, instrumentally useful competence.
BREW 3010.d: Students in this course investigate the malting, brewing, fermentation, and aging processes as they are related to historical and modern beer styles. Students apply an awareness of beer styles to the principles of beer and food pairing. Critical to the course is student practice of the sensory taste experience to map the aspects of beer and how the taste experience relates to beer style and the method served. Students compare the interpretation of historical beer styles to the current United States craft brewing industry.

r: The applied work is perceptual and diagnostic: illustrating the biological and chemical bases of aroma and taste, executing hedonic and analytical sensory-evaluation procedures on a trained panel, and troubleshooting beer faults back to their source in the brewing process. These map to O*NET activities like Inspecting or Evaluating Materials Against Standards and Identifying Objects, Actions, and Events, perceptual discrimination that task-exposure research places well outside AI's automatable range, analogous to trained clinical listening. An instrument or model can report a compound concentration, but it does not develop or replace the human panelist's calibrated palate, and misattributing a fault carries real cost, keeping the verification burden with a knowledgeable human. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire hands-on sensory competence is unaffected; embodiment and verification burden both protect it.

By 2031, gas chromatography, sensor arrays, and AI models correlating chemistry to flavor will grow more capable and offload some analytical fault-detection, augmenting the quality lab. But the graded competence, a human developing the perceptual acuity to detect, describe, and trace off-flavors and to judge hedonic acceptability, is embodied and real-time, and the jagged-frontier concern is acute: a plausible but wrong automated fault call, non-obviously mistaken, misdirects a whole brew's corrective action. There is no licensure lock; the protection is intrinsic to the sensory task. Diffusion of instrumented sensory analysis into craft-scale quality programs is partial. The instrumental case remains essentially intact at Low, with the caveat that routine analytical measurement is the most plausible thing to shift toward automation, not the trained-panel judgment.

A decade out, analytical instrumentation and chemistry-to-flavor prediction may handle much routine fault screening in well-resourced production labs, and the course could lean further toward interpretation over description. Even so, the specific competence Sensory Quality Analysis builds, a student personally cultivating the perceptual discrimination to evaluate beer and locate faults, is embodied and not executed by AI on the learner's behalf, so direct substitution stays low through 2036 in the central case. Verification demands persist because sensory judgments feed consequential process corrections. The honest uncertainty is how much descriptive measurement automates around a still-human evaluative core, not whether the trained palate remains instrumentally necessary. The rating holds Low, anchored by embodiment and by the real error cost of misjudged sensory assessment.
BREW 3810.d: In this course, students illustrate the biological and chemical principles that lead to aromatic, taste, and taste expressions in beer. Students practice procedures for hedonic and analytical sensory evaluation of beer. Students troubleshoot and process trace beer faults to their source in the brewing process.

r: Despite hands-on brewing, this course's core applied work is managerial and analytical: drafting the components of a brewery startup business plan, integrating World-Class Manufacturing pillars (Focused Improvement, 5S, Quality Control, Cost Deployment, Logistics), designing brewing and retail layouts for workflow, and benchmarking operational models against WCM standards. These map to O*NET activities like Developing Objectives and Strategies, Organizing and Planning Work, and Analyzing Data or Information, business-and-operations tasks that observed-usage data shows are a meaningful and growing share of AI use and that resemble the exposed management content in the calibration set. At 24 months, however, curricular restructuring is negligible and the integrative judgment of assembling a coherent operational plan is not yet reliably AI-executed end to end, so the instrumental need is only partly eroded. Rating Medium, with no licensure lock protecting it.

By 2031, AI will competently draft business-plan sections, generate layout options, populate cost and logistics analyses, and benchmark against manufacturing frameworks, materially reducing the routine execution this course's knowledge is applied to. The instrumental case erodes toward specifying, integrating, and verifying AI-generated operational plans rather than producing them from scratch. With no accreditation or licensure lock and only modest foundational scaffolding (it feeds the applied-operations capstone), little caps the rise, and the rating moves to High. The hedge: the WCM-integration and strategy-execution judgment the course cultivates retains value for oversight, and diffusion into small craft operations lags capability, so High reflects strong task automatability rather than the course becoming worthless; the planning artifacts, specifically, are what AI increasingly produces.

A decade out, the central case has AI competently generating brewery business plans, operational models, and WCM-benchmarked layout and cost analyses, so the execution rationale for teaching students to produce these documents is substantially eroded. What remains is the human judgment to specify constraints, integrate strategy with operations, and catch where an AI-generated plan is internally inconsistent or infeasible at a specific site. With no institutional lock and a terminal-to-modest foundational role, the rating holds High. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much of operations education shifts from producing plans to auditing AI-produced ones, and how fast capable tools diffuse into capital-thin craft breweries, not whether these planning and analysis tasks are highly exposed; the evidence indicates they are.
BREW 3850.d: In this course, students identify and describe the essential components of a business plan for a brewery startup, with a focus on integrating the 11 pillars of World-Class Manufacturing. They explain how these components influence the design of brewing and retail spaces, applying principles such as Focused Improvement, Workplace Organization (5S), and Quality Control to optimize layout and workflow. Through hands-on brewing, students apply scientific and technological concepts to ensure product quality, incorporating Autonomous Maintenance and Early Equipment Management to extend equipment life and reduce downtime. Students also analyze the interdependencies between business strategy and operational execution, including Safety, Cost Deployment, and Logistics. Students evaluate the effectiveness of their brewery plans by benchmarking against WCM standards and design comprehensive operational models that reflect best practices in People Development, Environment, and Professional Maintenance. The course culminates in an integrative project where students synthesize their learning into a scalable, sustainable brewery concept aligned with world-class performance metrics.

r: The applied work blends embodied sensory and hospitality-service tasks: analyzing and evaluating beer flavor via open and blind tasting, recognizing and assessing flavors, configuring and maintaining draft systems, selecting glassware and packaging, applying beer-and-food pairing, and delivering customer service in a beverage-presentation setting. These map to O*NET activities like Performing for or Working Directly with the Public, Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships, and perceptual Inspecting or Evaluating, categories task-exposure research places among the low-exposure interpersonal and physical bands. A model can draft pairing menus or service scripts, but it cannot taste blind, pull a clean pour, service a draft line, or read and respond to a guest in real time. At 24 months the instrumental need to develop embodied tasting and live service competence is unaffected; embodiment protects it, with no licensure lock required.

By 2031, AI will readily generate pairing recommendations, style descriptions, and service-training content, automating the knowledge-preparation layer. But the graded competencies, perceptual flavor assessment through tasting and real-time in-person hospitality service including draft-system operation and guest interaction, are embodied and interpersonal, keeping a trained human necessary. The dampening effect of that presence holds the rating at Low even as the informational tasks rise with capability. There is no accreditation or licensure lock; the protection is intrinsic to the sensory-and-service nature of the work, and diffusion of any automation into hands-on beverage service is limited. The honest hedge is that content generation for menus and training migrates to AI, while the live tasting-and-serving competence the course builds does not.

A decade out, AI will supply sophisticated pairing logic, style knowledge, and service documentation on demand, substantially eroding the preparation rationale. Yet the specific competence Beer Styles and Service develops, a student personally cultivating a discriminating palate and effective live beverage service, is embodied and interpersonal, not a task AI executes for the learner, so direct substitution stays low through 2036 in the central case. With no institutional lock and a terminal role, the rating holds Low anchored by embodiment rather than mandate. The plausible decade-scale change is in how much menu design, inventory, and training content automates around a still-human tasting-and-hospitality core, not in whether embodied service and sensory skill remain instrumentally necessary; the low-exposure evidence indicates they do.
BREW 4010.d: In this course, students will identify and explain the key conditions and components of the brewing process that contribute to the distinctive flavor profiles of various beer styles. Through guided instruction and experiential learning, students will analyze and evaluate sensory characteristics using both open and blind tasting methodologies, developing advanced skills in flavor recognition and assessment. Students will compare and contrast draft system configurations, including service protocols, glassware selection, and packaging components. Emphasis will be placed on the application and evaluation of appropriate design principles, operational procedures, and maintenance strategies to ensure optimal product delivery and customer satisfaction. Additionally, students will describe and apply foundational principles of beer and food pairing, considering flavor balance, intensity, and complementary profiles. They will also demonstrate effective customer service techniques tailored to beverage presentation and hospitality settings, fostering professional communication and service excellence.

r: The applied work is laboratory and process microbiology: culturing and pitching yeast, bacterial and mixed cultures; safely handling microorganisms; and collecting, storing, and managing yeast to ensure the quality and style-appropriateness of finished beer, complemented by lab activities on fermentation biology. These map to O*NET activities like Controlling Machines and Processes, Handling and Moving Objects, Monitoring Processes and Materials, and Documenting Information, hands-on wet-lab work that task-exposure research places well outside AI's automatable range, analogous to a chemistry laboratory. A model can explain fermentation kinetics or design a pitching schedule, but it cannot maintain a sterile field, propagate a healthy culture, or catch a contamination event at the bench. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire safe, competent fermentation-lab technique is unaffected; embodiment and contamination-error risk both protect it.

By 2031, AI-assisted fermentation modeling, sensor-driven monitoring, and lab-information tools will grow more capable and inform pitch rates, temperature schedules, and yeast-management decisions, augmenting the process-control layer. But the graded competence, physically culturing, handling, and storing living organisms under aseptic technique and judging culture health, is embodied and carries real biosafety and spoilage consequences, exactly where the jagged-frontier caution about mis-calibrated trust in automated output applies. There is no licensure lock; protection is intrinsic to the wet-lab task. Diffusion of automated fermentation control into craft-scale operations is partial and uneven. The instrumental case stays Low at five years, with the honest caveat that process-monitoring analytics and scheduling are the plausible things to shift toward AI, not the hands-on microbiological technique.

A decade out, instrumented and partly automated fermentation control will be more common in larger breweries, and AI will strongly support process decisions. Even so, the specific competence Brewing Fermentation builds, a student personally acquiring aseptic culture handling, yeast management, and fermentation-lab judgment, is embodied and not executed by AI on the learner's behalf, so direct substitution stays low through 2036 in the central case, and contamination-error verification keeps a knowledgeable human necessary. The genuine uncertainty is how much routine monitoring and scheduling automates around a still-human bench core, not whether hands-on fermentation-microbiology technique remains instrumentally necessary. The rating holds Low, anchored by embodiment and by the real cost of a mishandled culture; craft-scale operations especially retain human-run cellar work.
BREW 4220.d: Students are introduced to an overview of the modern and traditional brewing fermentation processes. Laboratory activities and assignments complement course activities related to the microbiology of fermentation and brewing with yeast, bacterial and mixed cultures. Students review the process of fermenting with yeast, bacteria, and mixed cultures. In addition to the process of fermentation, students engage in the collection, storage, and handling of yeast to assure both safe handling of microorganisms and the quality and appropriateness of style of the finished beer.

r: The applied work is hands-on production and analysis: pilot-batch brewing of major beer styles, monitoring the brewing process, and analyzing intermediate and final beers to connect brewing science and engineering technology to practice, the art-and-science link the course foregrounds. These map to O*NET activities like Controlling Machines and Processes, Monitoring Processes and Materials, and Analyzing Data or Information. The production and process-monitoring core is embodied and real-time, which task-exposure research places among the low-exposure categories, while the analytical strand is more exposed. A model can compute a mash profile or interpret gravity data, but it cannot run the pilot system, make live process adjustments, or develop the student's felt sense of how a brew is progressing. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire hands-on brewing-technology competence is unaffected; embodiment dampens exposure.

By 2031, AI will readily perform recipe formulation, predict process outcomes, and interpret beer-analysis data, automating the computational and design strands this course also teaches. But the graded competence, physically executing pilot brews, monitoring and adjusting the process in real time, and building the embodied judgment linking science to sensory outcome, resists substitution, and a confident-but-wrong automated process call carries real batch-loss cost, keeping verification with the trained brewer. There is no licensure lock; protection is intrinsic to the production task, and the course also scaffolds the applied-operations capstone. The instrumental case stays Low at five years, with the honest caveat that recipe design and data analysis are the plausible things to shift toward AI, not the hands-on brewing execution the course centers.

A decade out, AI will strongly support recipe development, process optimization, and beer analysis, and instrumented brewhouses will automate more monitoring in capital-rich plants. Even so, the specific competence Applied Brewing Science and Technology builds, a student personally running pilot brews, adjusting live processes, and internalizing the science-to-sensory connection, is embodied and not executed by AI on the learner's behalf, so direct substitution stays low through 2036 in the central case. The genuine uncertainty is how much formulation and analysis automate around a still-human brewing core, not whether hands-on brewing-technology competence remains instrumentally necessary. The rating holds Low, anchored by embodiment; craft-scale pilot brewing in particular remains a human, hands-on activity even as analytical tools mature.
BREW 4350.d: Students structure the foundational knowledge of brewing science and technology principles based on science and engineering technology. The course activities include pilot batch brewing of major beer styles and analysis of the intermediate and final beers. Students monitor the brewing process to develop skills in brewing technology and an awareness of the connection between the art and science of brewing.

r: This capstone integrates business and embodied work: students synthesize operational, promotional, technical, talent-management, and sensory aspects of commercial beer production, deliver a written and oral product plan with a finished beer, direct their peers in large-batch production, and publicly propose and promote the product for the marketplace. The business strands map to O*NET activities like Developing Objectives and Strategies, Selling or Influencing Others, and Communicating with Persons Outside the Organization, exposed managerial and promotional work, while directing peers in physical production and presenting live map to Guiding and Motivating Subordinates and Performing General Physical Activities, which are embodied and interpersonal. At 24 months the integrative, team-led production and live promotion are not AI-executed, and the embodiment dampens the exposed business layer, so the instrumental need is largely intact. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI will competently draft product plans, promotional campaigns, financial projections, and operational schedules, automating much of the document-and-analysis layer this capstone requires. But the graded synthesis, leading peers through an actual large-batch brew, presenting and defending a plan live, and delivering a finished beer, is embodied, real-time, and interpersonal, keeping the human competence necessary and dampening the exposed strands. With no licensure lock and a terminal capstone role, the protection is intrinsic to the production-and-leadership task rather than institutional. The instrumental case holds at Low, with the honest hedge that the promotional, financial, and planning artifacts are precisely what AI increasingly produces, so the balance of the course tilts toward the still-human execution and integration as those pieces automate.

A decade out, the central case has AI competently generating the business, promotional, and operational content this capstone integrates, so the execution rationale for those strands is substantially eroded, lifting base automatability. What resists is the embodied core, directing a real production team, executing a large batch, and defending a product live to an audience, which AI does not perform on the learner's behalf; embodiment dampens the rise but no longer fully offsets it, so the rating moves to Medium. With no institutional lock, the protection is the physical-and-interpersonal nature of the capstone alone. The genuine uncertainty is how much of producing a beer for the marketplace becomes AI-drafted planning around a still-human production-and-leadership act, not whether those planning tasks are exposed; they are.
BREW 4850.d: This course is an application of both theoretical and practical product development skills in the brewing industry. Students synthesize their knowledge by completing a critical analysis of the operational, promotional, technical, talent management, and sensory aspects of commercial beer production. The principal outcome of the course is a written and oral presentation of a product plan, and a finished beer. Students direct their peers and are evaluated in the large batch production of a beer inclusive of the skillset gained in prior coursework to include the financial, promotional, and operational, and managerial requirements of beer production. Students publicly propose and promote their beer product to demonstrate their mastery the comprehensive aspects of planning and producing a beer for the marketplace.
